How to Make a Friendship Bracelet
A friendship bracelet is a fun way to show a friend you care.
You will need:
three pieces of coloured wool, each as long as your arm
sticky tape
Steps:
1. Tie the three pieces together with a knot at one end.
2. Tape the knot to a table.
3. Plait the wool. Cross the left piece over the middle one, then the right piece over the middle one. Keep going.
4. When it fits around a wrist, tie another knot.
5. Give it to your friend with a big smile.
Tip: Choose your friend's favourite colours. They will know you were thinking of them!

The Man Who Gave Us Kindergarten
Friedrich Froebel was born in Germany in 1782. As a boy, he loved exploring the forest near his home. He studied plants, rocks and animals.
When he grew up, Froebel became a teacher. He noticed that young children learnt best when they were playing.
In 1837, he opened a special school for little children. They sang songs, played games and built with wooden blocks. They also grew flowers in a garden.
Froebel called his school a kindergarten. In German, this means 'children's garden'. Today, kindergartens are found all over the world.

Protect Our Seagrass Meadows
Under the shallow water in some bays, there are green meadows of seagrass. We must look after them!
Seagrass is home to baby fish, crabs and seahorses. It hides them from hungry hunters. Dugongs, also called sea cows, munch on seagrass every day. Without it, they would go hungry.
Sadly, boat anchors and propellers can tear the seagrass out. It grows back very slowly.
Boaties, please drop your anchor on sand, not grass. Go slowly in shallow water. Let's keep the meadows green!

Small Squares of the World
A stamp is a tiny picture you stick on a letter to pay for its trip. Some people collect them.
Stamps show all sorts of things, like animals, sports stars and famous places. A stamp from Japan might show a mountain. One from Kenya might show a lion.
Collectors keep stamps in special books called albums. They use tweezers to pick them up, because fingers can bend the edges or leave marks.
Some stamps are very rare. Only a few were ever made, so collectors will travel a long way just to see one.
QuestionText: What do collectors keep their stamps in?
